opis: Bread on the table, a lamp in the night, and the smoke of prayer: what the daily life of the sanctuary says about Jesus and about us.

teksty.p1: Exodus 25:23-24, 29-30; Leviticus 24:5-9; John 6:30-35; Exodus 25:31-33, 37; Exodus 26:35; Exodus 27:20-21; John 8:12; John 1:4-5, 9; John 12:46; Exodus 30:1, 6-8; Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; Revelation 8:3-4
teksty.p2: Deuteronomy 8:3; John 6:48-51; Jeremiah 1:11-12; Zechariah 4:1-6; Ephesians 5:8-9; Luke 1:8-10

zdanie: In God’s house there was always bread, a lamp was always burning, and the smoke of prayer was always rising. God doesn’t close His house for the night.

elementy.tekst: This meeting takes place in the first room of the sanctuary, the Holy Place. Three pieces of furniture stood there: the table with the bread, the lampstand, and the small golden altar for burning incense. Nothing there was reserved for special occasions. The bread was always there, the lamp burned every night, and incense was burned morning and evening. If the lamp is lit, the bread is on the table, and fragrant smoke hangs in the air, it means someone is home. The group should first see these three things with their own eyes, and then hear Jesus say, “I am the bread” and “I am the light.”

A related meeting is “The God Who Wants to Live with Us” in The Secret of the Early Church series. That one asks why God came to live in a tent at all. This one goes inside and looks at what happened there every day.
**Where the landmines are:**

pozycje: Jesus’ words about bread can easily lead into a dispute about the Lord’s Supper and how different churches understand it. There may be Catholics and Orthodox Christians at the table. Don’t settle that today. Stay with what the text says. Jesus calls people to come to Him and believe in Him.
For many people, incense is connected with worship in their own church. Don’t judge anyone’s practice. The Bible uses incense as a picture of prayer, and that is what you are talking about.
The symbolism of the furniture tempts people to look for meaning in every bud of the lampstand. The text says little, and that is enough.
Someone at the table may have been through a night in which they saw no light at all. The words “will never walk in the darkness” must not sound like an accusation that they don’t believe enough.

elementy.tekst: **What not to do:** don’t give a lecture on the measurements of the table and the lampstand. Don’t judge who prays well and who prays badly. Don’t promise that faith removes every darkness.
What ordinary thing in your home gives you the feeling that you’re where you belong? A smell, a light in the window, something on the table. One word is enough.
answer first, and keep it short, to set the length. Don’t comment on anyone else’s answer.

bloki.tytul: A Table That Was Always Set

elementy.tekst: On Mount Sinai, God gives Moses a description of the sanctuary, the tent in which He will live among His people. A table is to stand in the first room.

akapity: You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it. … You are also to make the plates and dishes, as well as the pitchers and bowls for pouring drink offerings. Make them out of pure gold. And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times.

You are also to take fine flour and bake twelve loaves, using two-tenths of an ephah for each loaf, and set them in two rows—six per row—on the table of pure gold before the LORD. And you are to place pure frankincense near each row, so that it may serve as a memorial portion for the bread, an offering made by fire to the LORD. Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant. It belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place; for it is to him a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD—his portion forever.”

elementy.tekst: Twelve loaves, as many as the tribes of Israel, lie on the table “before Me at all times.” **What does it mean that the people are present before God in the form of ordinary bread?**
The bread is replaced once a week, on the Sabbath, and the priests eat the old loaves. **Who ends up being fed by this bread? What does that say about who is feeding whom here?**
Frankincense is placed with the bread as a “memorial portion.” **Who is meant to remember what here?**

In the temples of the surrounding nations, the gods were served food every day, at human mealtimes, along with something to drink. In the sanctuary, the bread was replaced only once a week, and the priests ate it. The God of Israel doesn’t need food. He is the one who feeds. The Hebrew name of the bread literally means “bread of the face,” because it lay before the face of the LORD. That is why English Bibles call it the Bread of the Presence.

Morning and evening a priest went into the Holy Place. He tended the lamps of the lampstand and burned incense on the golden altar. At the same time a lamb was offered in the courtyard. In the later temple, the people gathered for prayer at these hours. The tent was covered with heavy curtains, so no daylight got inside. Only the lampstand gave light. Once a week, on the Sabbath, fresh bread was placed on the table. The Hebrew word that the BSB renders “at all times,” “continually,” or “perpetually” is `tamid`. It is used of the bread, of the lamp, and of the incense.
**What does a house where the light never goes out, the table is never empty, and prayer never falls silent say about God?**

bloki.tytul: The Bread That Comes Down from Heaven

elementy.tekst: The day after Jesus fed the crowd with bread and fish, the people find Him on the other side of the lake.

akapity: So they asked Him, “What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You? What will You do? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.” Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.

elementy.tekst: The people ask for a sign and bring up the manna. **What does Jesus correct in the way they remember it? Who really gave the bread?**
“Give us this bread at all times.” Instead of another meal, Jesus gives them Himself. **What do these people want, and what is He offering them?**
“Whoever comes to Me will never hunger.” **How do you understand this sentence, when believers still find themselves hungry for God?**

The bread on the table in the sanctuary lay before God on behalf of the people. The people brought the flour, and God gave the bread back to the priests to eat. Jesus turns the direction around even further. The bread doesn’t go from people to God. It comes down from God to people and gives “life to the world.” You don’t have to earn it or bake it. You have to come.

akapity: He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

elementy.tekst: Moses speaks of the hunger in the wilderness as a kind of school. **What was God teaching His people by feeding them day by day instead of giving them a supply in advance?**
The bread Jesus speaks of costs Him His life: “this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.” **What does that change in the words “bread of life”?**

bloki.tytul: A Lamp That Burns at Night

akapity: Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold. It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. Six branches are to extend from the sides of the lampstand—three on one side and three on the other. There are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extend from the lampstand. … Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it.
And place the table outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle, and put the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side.

And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually. In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come.

elementy.tekst: The lampstand looks like a branch of an almond tree, with cups and blossoms. **Why does the light in God’s house grow out of something that looks like a living tree?**
The lamps are to burn “from evening until morning.” **Why does God care so much about light at night in particular?**
The lampstand stands opposite the table, and its lamps “illuminate the area in front of it.” The oil is brought by ordinary people. **What does this light fall on, and who helps keep it burning?**

The table with the twelve loaves stood opposite the lampstand. So the light of the lamps fell on the loaves, one for each tribe. You can read this as a picture of the whole people in God’s light. Most of the rituals in the sanctuary took place during the day. About the lamp, the text says plainly that it is to burn from evening until morning. God kept watch over His people while they slept.

akapity: And the word of the LORD came to me, asking, “Jeremiah, what do you see?” “I see a branch of an almond tree,” I replied. “You have observed correctly,” said the LORD, “for I am watching over My word to accomplish it.”

elementy.tekst: In Hebrew, the almond is `shaqed`, and “I am watching” is `shoqed`. In Israel the almond tree is the first to blossom, while it is still late winter, as if it woke up before all the others.
**What does it add to the picture of the lampstand that its blossoms belong to the tree whose name sounds like “watching”?**

akapity: Then the angel who was speaking with me returned and woke me, as a man is awakened from his sleep. “What do you see?” he asked. “I see a solid gold lampstand,” I replied, “with a bowl at the top and seven lamps on it, with seven spouts to the lamps. There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left.” “What are these, my lord?” I asked the angel who was speaking with me. “Do you not know what they are?” replied the angel. “No, my lord,” I answered. So he said to me, “This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts.

elementy.tekst: The prophet asks about the lampstand, and the answer is about the Spirit. **What does “not by might nor by power” mean for someone who feels their light is growing dim?**

Later in this vision, the oil flows on its own from the trees standing beside the lampstand, through golden pipes into the lamps. **When in your life did something keep shining even though you no longer had the strength to keep it going?**
Jesus is in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly after the Feast of Tabernacles. He is teaching near the treasury, in the courtyard where everyone comes and goes (John 7:2; 8:20).

akapity: Once again, Jesus spoke to the people and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. … The true Light who gives light to every man was coming into the world.
I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness.

elementy.tekst: Jesus doesn’t say, “I will show you the light.” He says, “I am the light.” **What does that mean for someone trying to find their way in the dark?**

The lamp in the sanctuary shone inside a closed tent, before the eyes of a few priests. Jesus speaks of a light for the world, a light that gives light to “every man.” **What changes when the light comes out of the tent?**
“The darkness has not overcome it.” **How does this sentence sound to someone who is in the dark right now and can’t see a way out?**

Later Jewish sources describe great lampstands being lit in the temple courtyard during the Feast of Tabernacles, and their glow could be seen across the whole city. Jesus says His sentence in the same temple, in the days when that light was still fresh in people’s memory. Before, the lamp in the Holy Place shone only for the priests. Now the light stands in the courtyard, among the people, and calls out, “Whoever follows Me.”

akapity: For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.

elementy.tekst: Paul puts it strongly: “you were once darkness.” **How can someone who was darkness themselves give light?**
The fruit of the light consists in “all goodness, righteousness, and truth.” **How would the people around you recognize that a lamp is burning in you?**

akapity: “You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense. … Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony—before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony—where I will meet with you. And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come.
May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering.

elementy.tekst: In a vision, the apostle John sees heaven as a temple, with God’s throne and a golden altar.

akapity: When He had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.

Then another angel, who had a golden censer, came and stood at the altar. He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel.

elementy.tekst: The altar of incense stands closest to the veil, at the place “where I will meet with you.” **What does this location say about prayer?**
The psalmist asks that his prayer be set before God “like incense.” **What does the image of smoke say about prayer, about what can be seen and what can’t?**

In heaven, the golden bowls are full of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints,” and the angel “was given much incense” to offer along with the prayers. **What does this scene say about prayers that seem weak to us?**
Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was an ordinary priest. One day the lot chose him to serve at the altar of incense.

akapity: One day while Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God, he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And at the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside.

elementy.tekst: The priest goes in alone, and the whole congregation prays outside. **What connects these people with what is happening inside?**
**When you pray alone, what helps you remember that your prayer goes up together with the prayers of others?**

bloki.tytul: Tension: Does Prayer Need Something Added?

akapity: In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

elementy.tekst: In Revelation 5:8 the incense is the prayers of the saints themselves. In Revelation 8:3 incense is given to the angel and added to the prayers. Christians read this picture in two ways. Some see the incense simply as prayer, going up to God as in the psalm. Others, including many Adventists, see the incense added to the prayers as a picture of Christ’s intercession. In their view, our prayers reach God because of who Jesus is and what He has done. Both sides agree on two things. Prayer doesn’t reach God because of our eloquence or our strength. And intercession doesn’t mean the Father has to be persuaded to love us. God loved us before anyone interceded for us.
**What difference does it make to your prayer that the Spirit “intercedes for us” when you yourself don’t know what to ask for?**
**How can we talk about Jesus’ intercession without ending up with a picture of a God who first has to be talked into it?**

The bread, the lamp, and the incense came around day after day and week after week, repetitive to the point of boredom. **What in your faith happens in an ordinary way, day after day, and what would happen if it went out?**
**What do you need most right now: bread, light, or a prayer that reaches God? Why?**
If you’d like to share, **at what time of day does prayer come most easily to you, and when is it hardest?**

bloki.tytul: A Question Without an Easy Answer

elementy.tekst: **For centuries the priests did the same things every day: oil, wick, incense, and every week the bread. Where does faithfulness in repetition end and ritual without a heart begin? How can you tell in yourself?**

there’s no single answer here. It helps if someone notices that God Himself set up this daily rhythm. Repetition is not the enemy of faith. It becomes dangerous only when we forget whom we are doing it for.
In God’s house there was always bread, a lamp was always burning, and the smoke of prayer was always rising. God doesn’t close His house for the night.
**Verse to remember:** John 8:12 or Psalm 141:2.
Think about what you feed on when you’re hungry inside. Name for yourself **one thing that promises to fill you but leaves you hungry**.
The lamp in the sanctuary burned from evening until morning. When you turn off the light in the evening, remind yourself that **your night is not dark to God**. Stay with that thought for a moment.
**For the brave:** bring God a prayer you’re ashamed of, because it’s short, clumsy, or full of complaints. The psalm says that this prayer, too, can be set before Him like incense.

**“So is the bread of life Communion?”** Or a dispute about the Lord’s Supper. Christians understand the link between John 6 and the Supper in different ways, and that isn’t today’s topic. Say so calmly. Go back to the words you read about coming to Jesus and believing in Him. Everyone at the table can agree on that.

**“In our church they use incense. Is that good or bad?”** Don’t judge. The Bible knows incense in the sanctuary and in heaven as a picture of prayer. Today you are talking about what that picture says about prayer. Leave church customs for another time.

**Someone looks for meaning in every bud and blossom of the lampstand.** Thank them and go back to what the text says plainly: the lampstand is shaped like a tree in bloom, it shines through the night, and its light falls on the bread. That’s enough for the whole meeting.

**“I follow Jesus, and I still have darkness inside me.”** Don’t correct this person, and don’t give a quick answer. Point out that the lamp in the sanctuary shone precisely at night, and that John writes that the darkness has not overcome the light. He doesn’t write that there is no darkness. If someone talks about long-lasting hopelessness or thoughts of not wanting to live, talk with them after the meeting and encourage them to get professional help. Help them reach a crisis line in your country, and in an emergency, your local emergency number.

**“I don’t know how to pray. My prayers don’t get anywhere.”** That’s a common and honest thing to say. Don’t give instructions. Read Romans 8:26 or Psalm 141:2 again, and ask what this person hears in those words.

**Someone talks about the Sabbath as a measure of who is faithful.** The bread passage mentions the Sabbath. Don’t turn that into a test for anyone at the table. The text speaks of God, who renews the covenant table every week. It says nothing about judging people.
**You’re running out of time.** Skip block 3. Blocks 1, 2, 4, and 5 carry the meeting: the table, Jesus as the bread, Jesus as the light, and prayer like incense.
